extracted.intended_audience: aspiring and professional fiction writers and readers interested in an author's writing process
extracted.subtask_description: A practicing novelist's account of daily habits, tools, and draft-based workflow for producing commercial fiction; emphasizes discipline, solitude, and a three-draft method. Useful as prescriptive guidance for novel-length fiction production.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write every day
rubrics_metrics.description: I write every day. It’s just my job, and I’m very fortunate to love my job.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat writing as daily work: typically a regular work week with six to eight hours a day; sometimes a few hours on weekends. 'Every day' practice is the foundation of output and meeting deadlines. Anti-pattern: sporadic or excuse-driven writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discipline and routine are essential ('Routine is my god')
rubrics_metrics.description: Routine is my god. It’s what I do. A day or two off to recharge, then close the cage door and go again.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build and protect a daily schedule (early rising, dedicated work blocks, workouts, limited socializing). Routine enables high output and consistent progress. Anti-patterns: frequent events, social media, or activities that interrupt focused writing time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Work a consistent block of hours (6–8 hours typical)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the normal course of events, I work six to eight hours a day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect some of that time to be 'staring into space' (creative incubation) and research. Use sustained daily hours rather than relying on bursts. Scoring note: consistency and time-on-task are prioritized over sporadic sprinting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Solitary writing; minimal collaboration
rubrics_metrics.description: I love and treasure alone. I don’t brainstorm with other writers, with my editor or my agent on storylines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep the creative process solitary if that is your wiring; do not feel obligated to co-write or brainstorm collaboratively. Anti-pattern: forced brainstorming sessions if they disrupt your process.

rubrics_metrics.name: No ghostwriters / full personal authorship
rubrics_metrics.description: I do not, never have, never will use ghostwriters. My work is my work, start to finish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Insist on personal ownership of the text; readers deserve honesty about authorship. Anti-pattern: outsourcing core writing to others or misattributing authorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimal delegation—no staff or researchers
rubrics_metrics.description: I don’t have ‘staff’... I don’t use researchers because they’d annoy me.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do your own research and administrative work where feasible to avoid distractions and maintain control over detail. Delegation (e.g., staff, researchers) is acceptable for others, but for this author it is an anti-pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-draft method (first: discovery, second: revise, third: polish)
rubrics_metrics.description: I work on a three-draft method. The first draft, the discovery draft, the POS draft... Then I go back to page one for the second draft... When I finish the second draft, it’s time for the third, the last, the polish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First draft: get the story and characters down without revising. Second draft: fix, expand, work the language, test story cohesion. Third draft: polish, shore up sagging spots, spell-check, prepare to send to agent/editor. Anti-pattern: over-editing while drafting; skipping stages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not revise while writing the first draft
rubrics_metrics.description: I don’t go back in the writing of that first draft, fiddle and fix, I just plow on, get the story, the people, onto the page.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize completion of a discovery draft over iterative perfection. Trust that later drafts will fix problems. Anti-pattern: repeatedly reworking early pages and stalling progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Loose mental outline instead of formal outlining
rubrics_metrics.description: I don’t outline. I have a kind of loose mental outline, then I sit down, get started and hope it all works one more time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use whatever level of outlining works for you; this author prefers loose mental structure rather than detailed note cards or visual aids. Acknowledge that formal outlining is 'not wrong' and may be excellent for other writers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on core storytelling elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Am I getting the story out, are these people interesting, layered, human... Setting, pacing, character development and evolution, connections, relationships, transitions, conflicts, beats, hills and valleys, dialogue, description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate drafts primarily by how well they deliver these story elements. During revision, check whether characters are layered and human, pacing and transitions work, conflicts and beats land, and dialogue/description serve the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use simple tools; avoid distracting features
rubrics_metrics.description: I do all this work with my very, very old Word Perfect program... I like it doesn’t have bells and whistle that would get in my way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose writing tools that minimize distractions and unnecessary features. The goal is to keep focus on writing rather than on tool-driven interruptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect editorial input and be willing to revise
rubrics_metrics.description: My editor... works fast... I may have to stop the current work if Leslie wants any changes. Since she’s going to be right about those changes ninety-nine times out of a hundred, I don’t argue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain a respectful, trusting relationship with editors/agents; be prepared to implement requested changes. Anti-pattern: reflexively defending every choice instead of assessing editor feedback objectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect writing time from social media/time-sucks
rubrics_metrics.description: I don’t spend a lot of time, sometimes none at all, on social media. It’s a time suck. My time’s valuable to me.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit or eliminate social media and other distractions during productive writing periods. Treat these as low-value activities that reduce available writing time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain physical health as part of the process (90-minute daily workout)
rubrics_metrics.description: Then it’s time to go workout. 90 minutes, daily. That’s my routine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate regular exercise into the daily schedule to support stamina and creative thinking; physical routine complements writing discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be honest with readers—do not lie or misattribute
rubrics_metrics.description: I value and respect the reader. Lying, to me, equals devaluing and disrespect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uphold integrity in authorship and in representations to readers (e.g., authorship claims, marketing). Anti-pattern: deceptive practices that betray reader trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Productivity expectations: sustained high output possible
rubrics_metrics.description: At this time it’s being winged around I write five books a year. It’s actually four... I’m able to produce a lot of books because I work every day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High productivity is achieved through daily disciplined work, routine, and minimal outside commitments. Individual output will vary by writer and life circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three Ds: Discipline, Drive, Desire
rubrics_metrics.description: It’s discipline and drive and desire. The three Ds I also tout when asked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These qualities are emphasized as prerequisites for sustaining a professional writing career; talent alone is insufficient. Use them as motivational criteria when assessing commitment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct blunt advice to writers: stop making excuses
rubrics_metrics.description: Stop making excuses and write. Stop whining and write. Stop fucking around and write.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A straightforward admonition: prioritize action over excuses. This is presented as practical, no-nonsense behavioral advice rather than stylistic guidance.
